headline: 97 untouched Duck Hunt & Super Mario Bros. NES carts worth thousands discovered, 5 graded perfect 10
summary: A retro shop owner found 97 sealed NES cartridges, including Duck Hunt and Super Mario Bros., with five units receiving a perfect PSA 10 grade. These never-before-seen versions could fetch over $10,000 each at auction.
details: A retro shop owner in Waukesha, Wisconsin, discovered a rare stash of 97 untouched Nintendo Entertainment System (NES) cartridges. These included never-before-seen versions of popular games like Duck Hunt and Super Mario Bros., with five units achieving a perfect PSA 10 grade. Each cartridge is estimated to be worth $10,000 or more.

Kevin Braun, owner of OneStopWonders, bought the cartridges years ago from a seller whose grandfather salvaged precious metals from circuit boards. The box was meant for salvaging but ended up untouched in storage, initially valued by Braun at $10-$15 each.

The true value was realized when Braun's friend, Jason Ganos of Nintendo Wire, inspected them. Ganos shared the find in a high-end gaming Facebook group, attracting attention from directors at grading companies who requested further inspection.

Disassembly revealed these were among the last units produced in the 40th week of 1993. The manuals featured unique text ("maintenance or service" instead of "maintenance or repair"), confirming their rarity. PSA later authenticated the find in California.

The cartridges are believed to be replacements for warranty repairs, part of refurbished console bundles, or from an unreleased bundle. Nintendo of America has not confirmed their exact origin. Three of these rare carts will be auctioned at Goldin Auctions starting August 12.

While exact prices are unknown, estimates suggest at least four digits per cart, with perfect 10s potentially reaching five digits. Collectors may need a "war chest" of over $100,000 to secure one, drawing comparisons to an ultra-rare NES Gold Nintendo World Championships cartridge that sold for over $77,000.

headline_marked: [[China faces massive EV battery waste challenge]] as millions of cars near end-of-life
headline: China faces massive EV battery waste challenge as millions of cars near end-of-life
summary: China's booming EV market is creating a wave of retired batteries, with waste projected to hit 1.69 million metric tons by 2030, posing significant environmental and safety risks.
details: China's decade-long EV boom is leading to a major wave of battery retirements. Annual EV sales surged from 1 million in 2018 to over 16 million in 2025, with batteries typically lasting eight years. This marks the country's first significant period of mass battery disposal.

The volume of batteries needing disposal or reprocessing is expected to grow rapidly. China reported 400,000 metric tons of EV battery waste last year, projected to reach 1.69 million metric tons by 2030 and 22.39 million metric tons by 2040. This presents a massive waste-management and recycling challenge.

While EVs eliminate tailpipe emissions, critics argue their full life-cycle effects, including risks from discarded lithium-ion batteries, are a concern. Governments pushed EV adoption, betting recycling systems would eventually catch up.

China began building a formal recycling system in 2018, with over 150 companies since placed on the government’s certification “white list.” By 2023, these certified companies had a combined annual processing capacity of 623,000 metric tons, more than 1.5 times the volume of batteries retired that year.

However, certified recyclers handled only about 25% of retired batteries in 2023. Much of the used-battery supply still flows through uncertified recyclers, which poses serious environmental and safety risks due to improper disposal and contamination.

An investigation by Yicai found that over 100 certified companies were no longer operating or reachable. Researchers described China's effort to control the informal market as a "losing battle," citing poisoning, explosions, and environmental pollution from improper dismantling.

Informal operators can pay more for used batteries by avoiding costs associated with safe testing, dismantling, and pollution control. This makes selling to them more convenient for vehicle owners, undercutting certified businesses.

Retired batteries retain economic value and are rarely landfilled. Those in good condition can be repurposed for less demanding uses, while others can be recycled into raw materials for new batteries, but this requires proper testing and grading.
